And it teaches where courage actually lives: not in numbers or physique, but in two qualities Allah may place in any of His servants — fear of Him alone, and gratitude for His grace. Whoever fears Allah rightly finds every giant shrinking; whoever fears the giants has, for that moment, forgotten Who wrote the outcome.

passages.title: "We are staying here": the refusal and forty years of wandering
passages.tafsir:
This passage is the breaking point of the story that began in ayah 20. Mūsā (peace be upon him) has reminded the Children of Israel of Allah's favours, commanded them to enter the Holy Land, and two courageous men have shown them exactly how victory would come. Ayat 24–26 record what happened next: the community's final, absolute refusal; the prophet's anguished prayer when he realises he can count on no one but himself and his brother; and the divine sentence — forty years of wandering in the wilderness. What holds the three ayat together is a single courtroom-like exchange: the people speak (24), Mūsā speaks (25), and Allah gives His verdict (26).

## "Go, you and your Lord, and fight" — how far did the words go?

In ayah 22 the people had at least dressed their fear in an excuse: the land holds a mighty people; when *they* leave, *we* will enter. By ayah 24 even the excuse is gone. They say: "We will never enter it — *abadan*, ever — as long as they are there. So go, you and your Lord, and fight, you two; we are sitting right here." Ibn Kathir notes that the advice of the two Allah-fearing men — "assault them through the gate, and when you are in, victory will be yours" — "did not benefit them in the least." This was no longer hesitation; it was, in his words, how they "declined to join Jihad, defied their Messenger, and refused to fight their enemy."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān pauses over the exact wording, because it raises a real theological question. If "go, you and your Lord, and fight" had been said in mockery — as though the Lord were a comrade-in-arms to be sent off to battle — it would have been open disbelief (*kufr*). But Maʿārif points out an internal clue against that reading: the very next verse shows Mūsā still living with these people and praying for them in the wilderness of Tīh, which would not have been possible had they left the faith outright. So the leading commentators take the sense to be: "You go and fight; your Lord will help you. As for us, we cannot help you." On that reading the statement is not blasphemy — but it remains, as Maʿārif puts it, grotesque and hurtful, so notoriously so that the sentence became proverbial. Maʿārif adds the deeper charge. These were people who had watched Pharaoh and his court defeated on their own grounds at the hands of Mūsā and Hārūn, watched him drown while they themselves crossed the sea, and been handed the wealth of Egypt without any fighting or killing. For them to give their prophet this flat response at such a crucial moment was, Maʿārif says, to break all the pledges they had made.

## The mirror-image: Badr

The reason this ugly sentence "became proverbial" is that a later community was tested in almost the same way — and chose the opposite answer. Ibn Kathir sets the two scenes side by side. Before Badr, with a Quraysh army of nine hundred to a thousand approaching, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ kept asking, "Advise me, O Muslims!" Saʿd bin Muʿādh answered for the Ansar: "By He Who has sent you with the Truth! If you seek to cross this sea and went in it, we will follow you and none among us will remain behind… march forward with the blessing of Allah."

And the Companions themselves made the comparison explicit. Al-Bukhari records — in the Book of Al-Maghazi and At-Tafsir — from ʿAbdullah bin Masʿūd that on the day of Badr, Al-Miqdād said: "O Messenger of Allah! We will never say to you what the Children of Israel said to Mūsā, 'So go, you and your Lord, and fight, you two; we are sitting right here.' Rather, march on and we will be with you." The Prophet ﷺ was satisfied on hearing it. A similar report from Anas — that the Ansar swore, "If you took the camels to Bark Al-Ghimad (near Makkah) we shall follow you" — was recorded by Abu Bakr bin Marduwyah, and also by Imam Ahmad, An-Nasa'i and Ibn Hibban. Maʿārif adds a touching detail: Ibn Masʿūd used to say he envied Miqdād this one feat and wished the good fortune had been his. The Qur'an preserved the refusal of one people so that another people could consciously refuse to repeat it.

## Mūsā's prayer: "only myself and my brother"

In ayah 25 Mūsā turns from his people to his Lord: "My Lord, I have power only over myself and my brother." Ibn Kathir explains the sense: of this whole nation, only I and Hārūn will obey, carry out Allah's command and answer the call. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws attention to something easily missed: Yūshaʿ bin Nūn and Kālib bin Yūfannā — the two faithful men of ayah 23 — had stood with Mūsā throughout. Why does he not count them? Because, Maʿārif answers, Hārūn was a prophet and therefore divinely protected; his firmness was certain. The two chiefs, for all their proven loyalty, were not so protected and infallible — and Mūsā, in pain and anger after repeated breaches of trust, would now name before Allah only those whose steadfastness carried a guarantee. It is the prayer of a man who has been let down so many times that he will vouch for no one he cannot be certain of.

Then comes the petition itself: *fafruq baynanā wa bayna al-qawmi al-fāsiqīn*. The early authorities read it in two closely related ways. Al-ʿAwfī reported from Ibn ʿAbbās: "judge between us and them," and Ad-Dahhāk said similarly, "judge and decide between us and them" — a decisive distinguishing of the obedient from the rebellious. Other scholars took it as "separate between us and them." Maʿārif cites Ibn ʿAbbās's fuller explanation of its substance: give them the punishment they deserve, and give us whatever we are found to deserve. Either way, Mūsā is not cursing them with a specific doom; he is handing the matter entirely to Allah's justice. Note the word he chooses for them — *fāsiqīn*, "the rebellious people" — the very description with which Allah will close the next ayah.

## The verdict: a prison with no walls

Ayah 26 is Allah's answer: "Then it is forbidden to them for forty years; in distraction they will wander through the land." The scholars of tafsir cited in Maʿārif observe that Allah's punishment of a people is proportioned to their deed — and here it is proportioned even to their *words*. They had said, "we are sitting right here" (*innā hāhunā qāʿidūn*); so Allah made them sit right there, detained in that spot for forty years. The land they refused to enter was now *muḥarramah* — forbidden — to them: they could not go forward to the Holy Land, and, Maʿārif adds, they could not go back to Egypt either.

Ibn Kathir says they wandered about lost in the land of At-Tīh, "unable to find their way out." Maʿārif dwells on how astonishing this detention was. Citing the tafsir of Muqātil, it gives the area as roughly ninety miles by twenty-seven (by another account thirty by eighteen), and the people as six hundred thousand strong. Yet each evening, after a full day's march toward Egypt or toward Bayt al-Maqdis, they found themselves back where they had started in the morning, as if moving in a circle. Maʿārif draws the lesson beautifully: when Allah intends to detain someone, He needs no police, no handcuffs, no iron gates. The whole universe takes His orders, and open ground on every side becomes the jail.

## Mercy inside the punishment

Yet the Tīh was not only a prison, because Mūsā and Hārūn were inside it too. Ibn Kathir records that during this time tremendous miracles occurred: the clouds that shaded them, the manna and quails (*mann* and *salwā*) Allah sent down for them, and the water springs Allah brought forth from solid rock. It was also during these very years, he notes, that the Tawrah was revealed, the Law was established for the Children of Israel, and the Tabernacle of the Covenant was erected. Maʿārif attributes these mercies to the *barakah* — the blessing — of the presence of Mūsā and Hārūn among the people, together with the two favoured elders Yūshaʿ and Kālib: it was for their sake that blessings kept coming even during a period of detention and punishment. It details them lovingly — the canopy of clouds that followed them wherever they went; the special stone Mūsā would strike with his staff so that twelve streams gushed forth; the heavenly food when they hungered; and a tower of light for their nights. The generation was being punished, and simultaneously being taught, fed, shaded and given scripture. Maʿārif even suggests, since Allah is the Most Merciful of the merciful, that the people may have repented in that wilderness and that these blessings may have come partly in return for their repentance.

## How it ended — and the promise kept

The forty years were also a generational sentence. Ibn Abi Hatim recorded from Ibn ʿAbbās that during the wandering Mūsā and Hārūn died, as did everyone above forty years of age; Maʿārif's account agrees — Hārūn died first, and Mūsā about a year or six months later — and Allah then made Yūshaʿ bin Nūn a prophet over the survivors and the new generation. When the term ended, Yūshaʿ led them at last against Jerusalem. Ibn Kathir relates the famous scene: the city was falling on a Friday afternoon, and as the sun neared setting Yūshaʿ feared the Sabbath would begin, so he said, "You are commanded and I am commanded — O Allah, make it stop setting for me," and Allah held the sun until the conquest was complete. Ibn ʿAbbās's report adds the sequel of the war-booty: the fire would not consume the spoils, so Yūshaʿ announced that someone had committed theft from the booty, summoned the twelve leaders of the twelve tribes and took the pledge from them. The hand of one of them became stuck to Yūshaʿ's hand, and when Yūshaʿ told him, "You committed the theft, so bring it forth," the man brought a cow's head made of gold, with two eyes made of precious stones and a set of teeth made of pearls. Once it was added back to the booty the fire consumed it — for they were prohibited from keeping the spoils. Ibn Kathir remarks that there is evidence supporting all of this in the Sahih.

Maʿārif, reflecting on this ending, draws out the point that matters most. Allah had promised — *kataba Allāhu lakum* — that the Holy Land was destined for the Children of Israel, and that promise had to be fulfilled. What the refusing generation forfeited was not the promise but their own share in it: they were deprived of the victory for forty years, and the conquest came at the hands of their next generation, so that "the promise of Allah stood fulfilled." Disobedience delays and disqualifies people; it does not defeat Allah's decree.

## "Do not grieve for the rebellious people"

The ayah closes with words addressed to Mūsā's heart: *fa-lā ta'sa ʿalā al-qawmi al-fāsiqīn* — do not grieve over the rebellious people. Ibn Kathir gives its sense: do not feel sorrow or sadness over My judgment against them, for they deserve it. And yet the consolation itself is striking — this is the same Mūsā who had just prayed for separation from these people. Maʿārif explains why such comfort has a basis: the prophets, peace be upon them all, are endowed with a natural disposition that makes it impossible for them to bear the pain and hardship of their people, so that even when their people are punished, the prophets too are affected emotionally. The man who said "I have power only over myself and my brother" still needed Allah to console him over the very people who had wounded him. That is the measure of a prophet's heart.

## Living it

The passage's demand on the reader is contained in the contrast the Companions themselves drew. Every believer eventually stands where the Children of Israel stood: commanded toward something difficult, with the promise of Allah's help on one side and visible fear on the other. One community said, "Go, you and your Lord, and fight; we are sitting right here" — and sat for forty years. Another said, "March on, and we will be with you" — and Badr followed. And beneath it runs a sober warning about words: Allah took "we are sitting right here" literally. What we declare in a moment of cowardice or defiance can become the exact shape of our punishment — just as what we declare in a moment of trust, like Miqdād's declaration, can become the thing generations envy.

passages.title: The two sons of Adam: the rejected sacrifice
passages.tafsir:
# The Two Sons of Adam: The Rejected Sacrifice (5:27–29)

This passage opens the Qur'an's account of the first murder in human history. The Qur'an itself speaks only of "the two sons of Adam" (peace be upon him); it is the tafsir tradition that supplies their names — Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records that, by the judgment of the majority of authentic scholars of tafsir, the two meant here are the two real sons of Adam, Habil (Abel) and Qabil (Cain). What binds these three ayat together is a single scene: a sacrifice accepted from one brother and rejected from the other, a threat of murder born of envy, and the astonishing reply of the righteous brother who refuses to raise his hand even to save his own life. Ayah 27 sets the stage and states the principle on which everything turns; ayat 28–29 give the righteous brother's answer — first his refusal to retaliate, then his warning of where the crime will lead.

## Why this story, and why here

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that in the preceding verses, the Banī Isrāʼīl were commanded to fight in Allah's cause and responded with cowardice and evasion. Set directly against that failure, this story condemns the opposite extreme: killing unjustly. The Qur'an is steering its readers to balance — just as it is an error to shrink from fighting to uphold truth, it is equally a road to ruin, in this world and the Hereafter, to fight and kill without right.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān also observes that the Qur'an is not a book of folklore or history told for its own sake. It narrates the particular segment of an event that carries the lesson needed at that place — and this story carries many lessons, with religious teachings woven through it.

Ibn Kathir adds that the command "relate to them" is aimed pointedly at the envious and unjust; the story was to be recited to the People of the Book, or, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it, to the whole Ummah.

## "In truth" — a single word carrying a principle

Ayah 27 does not simply say "relate to them the story"; it says relate it **bil-ḥaqq** — *in truth*. Ibn Kathir explains this to mean: clearly and without ambiguity, alteration, confusion, change, addition or deletion. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out of this single word an enduring principle: great caution is mandatory when reporting historical accounts. A small change of wording can distort the reality of an event, and it was precisely through this trapdoor of negligence that the religious codes of past communities were lost, their scriptures reduced to collections of stories with no reliable authority. The Qur'an repeats this insistence elsewhere — "This is indeed the true narration" (3:62), "We narrate to you their story with truth" (18:13).

There is a second layer, too. The Prophet ﷺ was *ummiyy* — untaught by any human being — yet here he relates, with complete accuracy, events from thousands of years earlier. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out that this itself is a proof of revelation: how else could an unlettered man narrate ancient history "in truth" except that it was divinely revealed to him?

## The word *qurbān*

The brothers "offered a sacrifice" — in Arabic, *qarrabā qurbānan*. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that *qurbān*, in its root sense, is anything made a *medium of nearness* to someone; in Islamic legal usage it came to mean the sacrifice offered to seek nearness to Allah.

## The story behind the sacrifice

Why did two brothers offer sacrifices at all? Ibn Kathir relates, from scholars among the Salaf and later generations, the background — and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān presents it as the position Ibn Kathir declared agreed upon by earlier and later scholars.

When Adam and Hawwaʼ (peace be upon them) began having children, each pregnancy produced twins — a boy and a girl. Since there was no one on earth besides Adam's own children, Allah made a special provision in the law given to Adam: a boy could not marry his own twin sister, but could marry a sister from a different pregnancy. Ibn Abi Hatim recorded from Ibn 'Abbas — in a report Ibn Kathir describes as having "a better than good chain of narration" — that the woman was not allowed in marriage to her male twin, but Adam was commanded to marry her to one of her other brothers.

The girl born with Qabil was beautiful; the girl born with Habil was not. By the rule, the beautiful girl fell to Habil. Qabil was enraged and demanded her for himself. Adam refused — but to settle the dispute, he proposed that both sons offer a sacrifice to Allah: whoever's sacrifice was accepted would marry her. In those days the open sign of acceptance was that a fire would descend from the sky and consume the offering. Habil, a keeper of flocks, offered a fine spring lamb; Qabil, a farmer, offered some grain. The fire came down and consumed Habil's sacrifice; Qabil's lay untouched.

Humiliated and consumed by envy, Qabil turned on his brother with the naked threat recorded in ayah 27: *"I will surely kill you."*

## "Allah accepts only from those who have taqwā"

Habil's first reply is the axis of the whole passage. He does not answer anger with anger; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes his reply was peaceful, principled, and even carried an element of sympathetic concern: had you feared Allah, your sacrifice too would have been accepted — so why blame me?

This sentence — *"Allah accepts only from those who have taqwā"* (the fear and consciousness of Allah) — has, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it, the status of a foundational principle: the acceptability of deeds and acts of worship depends on taqwā. Two things follow from it.

**First, the cure for envy.** Tafsir Mazhari (cited in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān) draws this out: when the envier sees Allah has given someone a blessing withheld from him, he should treat his deprivation as the result of his own shortcomings and turn to repentance and self-correction — not scheme for the other person to lose the blessing, which brings the envier no gain and only loss. Qabil's whole tragedy is that he attacked the person who was blessed instead of correcting the deficiency in himself.

**Second, the fear of the righteous.** The Salaf lived in awe of this ayah. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān relates that 'Amir ibn 'Abdullah wept on his deathbed; when people reminded him of his lifetime of worship, he said this very verse was ringing in his ears — "I just do not know if any worship of mine will be accepted, or not." Ibn Abi Hatim recorded that Abu ad-Dardaʼ said that certainty that Allah had accepted even one prayer from him would be better for him than this world and all it contains. 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud said he would not trade the certainty of one accepted deed even if the whole world turned to solid gold in his possession. 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz wrote in a letter: hold on to taqwā, for without it no deed is accepted, no mercy is shown, and no reward is given — "There are many who preach it but there are very few who practice it." And Sayyidna al-Murtada (may Allah be pleased with him) said: even the smallest deed done with taqwā is not small — for how can a deed that has been *accepted* be called small?

## Ayah 28 — the hand that would not stretch

Habil's next words are among the most striking in the Qur'an: *"If you stretch your hand against me to kill me, I shall never stretch my hand against you to kill you, for I fear Allah, the Lord of all that exists."*

Ibn Kathir explains the meaning: I will not commit the same evil act you threaten, so that I do not earn the same sin as you; rather, I will observe patience and endurance. This was not weakness. 'Abdullah bin 'Amr said: "By Allah! Habil was the stronger of the two men. But fear of Allah restricted his hand." His restraint was chosen, and chosen out of fear of Allah — the same taqwā that had made his sacrifice acceptable now governed his hand.

Ibn Kathir connects this to the words of the Prophet ﷺ in a hadith recorded in the Two Sahihs: when two Muslims face each other with their swords, both the killer and the killed are in the Fire. The Companions asked — the killer, yes, but why the one killed? He ﷺ replied: because he too was intent on killing his companion. Habil's stance guards against exactly this: he refused even the *intention* of unjust killing.

The Sunnah then makes this righteous son of Adam an explicit model for later generations. Imam Ahmad recorded that at the beginning of the calamity that befell 'Uthman, Sa'd bin Abi Waqqas bore witness that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said there would be a *fitnah* (a time of violent civil discord) in which the one who sits is better than the one who stands, the one who stands better than the one who walks, and the one who walks better than the one who hastens. Asked, "What if someone enters my home and stretches out his hand to kill me?" he ﷺ answered: **"Be just like the (pious) son of Adam."** At-Tirmidhi also recorded it and graded it Hasan, noting similar reports from Abu Hurayrah, Khabbab bin al-Aratt, Abu Bakr, Ibn Mas'ud, Abu Waqid and Abu Musa. In times of fitnah between Muslims, this refusal is not merely admirable — it is the Prophet's ﷺ own prescription.

## Ayah 29 — "that you bear my sin and your sin"

Habil closes with a warning, not a curse: *"I want you to bear my sin as well as your own, and so become one of the dwellers of the Fire — and that is the recompense of the wrongdoers."*

What does "my sin and your sin" mean? Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Ad-Dahhak, As-Suddi and Qatadah — as recorded by Ibn Jarir — explained it as: *the sin of murdering me*, added on top of *your own previous sins*. Habil is not wishing damnation on his brother; he is stating the terrible arithmetic of murder. If you kill me, the burden of that killing falls entirely on you, stacked upon everything you already carry — and its end is the Fire. Even his last words are an attempt to talk his brother out of the crime.

## The sequel, in brief

The threat of ayah 27 was carried out, and Ibn Kathir's commentary on this passage includes the two ayat that record it (5:30–31): Qabil's soul made the murder seem fair to him, he killed his brother, and "became one of the losers" — in this life and the Hereafter, and, as Ibn Kathir asks, what loss is worse than that? Allah then sent a crow to scratch the ground and show him how to bury his brother's body, leaving him in regret.

Two reports in Ibn Kathir seal the story's weight. Imam Ahmad recorded from 'Abdullah bin Mas'ud that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: no soul is unjustly killed but that the first son of Adam carries a share of the burden of its blood, for he was the first to establish the practice of murder. The Group of hadith compilers, with the exception of Abu Dawud, also recorded it. And Ibn Jarir recorded that 'Abdullah bin 'Amr used to say that the son of Adam who killed his brother will be the most miserable among men: no blood is shed on earth, from that day until the Day of Resurrection, but he carries a burden from it, for he was the first person to establish murder.

Ibn Kathir closes with a teaching of the Prophet ﷺ: no sin is more deserving that Allah hasten its punishment in this world — on top of what is stored up for its doer in the Hereafter — than transgression and the severing of the ties of kinship. Qabil's act, Ibn Kathir observes, combined both: he transgressed, and he did it against his own brother.

## Living it

The passage asks something concrete of the believer. When you see another person blessed with what you were denied, look inward and repent — do not resent the blessed. Anchor your worship in taqwā, for acceptance, not volume, is what counts; the Salaf who worshipped most feared most for their acceptance. And when violence threatens — above all between believers — remember the Prophet's ﷺ answer to the man who asked what to do if someone entered his home to kill him: "Be just like the (pious) son of Adam." The one who refuses to stretch out his hand, out of fear of Allah, leaves the whole burden of the crime — the victim's blood on top of the killer's own sins — with the one who commits it.

passages.title: The murder, the crow, and the sanctity of every life
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat carry the story of Adam's two sons to its terrible conclusion and then draw out of it one of the most far-reaching declarations in the whole Qur'an. Ayah 30 is the murder — the first blood ever shed on earth. Ayah 31 is the crow, sent by Allah to teach the killer what to do with his brother's body. Ayah 32 is the verdict Allah Himself draws from the crime: a law, written for the Children of Israel and standing as a lesson for all who read it, that to kill one soul unjustly is as if one had killed all of mankind, and to save one is as if one had saved them all. What holds the passage together is this movement from a single crime to a universal principle — the Qur'an tells the story not as history for its own sake but, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it, because events of the past "carry many lessons and wise counsels within their fold," and beneath them lie religious injunctions.

## The story so far

The preceding ayat (27–29) set the scene. The two sons of Adam — identified as Habil (Abel) and Qabil (Cain), as Ibn Kathir says "many scholars among the Salaf and later generations" held — each offered a sacrifice to Allah; it was accepted from one and not the other. Ibn Kathir relates the background from several scholars among the Salaf and the later generations: in that first generation, Adam's children were born as twins, a boy and a girl in each pregnancy, and by a necessary provision Adam عليه السلام would give the girl of one twin-pair in marriage to the boy of another. Habil's sister was not beautiful while Qabil's sister was beautiful, and Qabil wanted her for himself instead of his brother; Adam refused unless they both offered a sacrifice, and he whose sacrifice was accepted would marry her. Ibn Abi Hatim records a report from Ibn ʿAbbas — which Ibn Kathir's tafsir grades as having "a better than good chain of narration" — telling the story without naming the brothers: a woman was not allowed in marriage to her own male twin; a beautiful daughter and one who was not beautiful were born to Adam; the twin brother of the ugly daughter proposed a swap — "Marry your sister to me and I will marry my sister to you" — and was refused; so both offered a sacrifice, and "the sacrifice of the one who offered the sheep was accepted while the sacrifice of the other... which consisted of some produce, was not accepted. So the latter killed his brother."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the fuller picture of the offering — an account it describes as reported on sound and strong chains of authorities and as what Ibn Kathir declared the agreed position of the earlier and later scholars. Habil owned a flock of sheep and goats and offered a good spring lamb; Qabil was a farmer and offered some grains. In those days the open sign of acceptance was that a fire would come from the sky and consume the sacrifice — and the fire ate up Habil's offering while Qabil's remained lying where it was, untouched. Enraged, Qabil said, "I will surely kill you" — and Habil answered with the sentence that became a principle for all time: "Allah accepts only from those who have taqwa" (fear of Allah). He then refused to raise his hand in return, saying, "If you do stretch your hand against me to kill me, I shall never stretch my hand against you to kill you, for I fear Allah, the Lord of all that exists." ʿAbdullah bin ʿAmr swore: "By Allah! Habil was the stronger of the two men. But fear of Allah restricted his hand."

## Ayah 30 — how a soul talks itself into murder

The Qur'an's wording is piercing: *fa-ṭawwaʿat lahu nafsuhu qatla akhīhi* — "his soul made the killing of his brother seem fair to him." Ibn Kathir explains: his conscience encouraged him and made the murder seem "like a sensible thing to do, so he killed him, even after his brother admonished him." The ayah does not say simply "he killed him"; it first shows us the inner surrender — the self dressing up an enormity until it looks reasonable.

The early authorities even preserved accounts of how the deed was done. Ibn Jarir relates that Qabil did not know how to kill — he began twisting his brother's neck — until Shaytan demonstrated with an animal, placing its head on a rock and smashing it with another stone while the son of Adam watched. In the narration of ʿAbdur-Rahman bin Zayd bin Aslam from his father (recorded by Ibn Abi Hatim), Shaytan then ran to Hawwa' (Eve) and told her, "Qabil killed Habil." She asked, "Woe to you! What does 'kill' mean?" He said, "He will no longer eat, drink or move." Death itself had to be explained to the first mother, because no human being had ever died. She wept — the first grief of the human family.

Then the verdict of the ayah: *fa-aṣbaḥa min al-khāsirīn* — "he became one of the losers." Ibn Kathir asks: losers in this life and the Hereafter — "and which loss is worse than this?" The murdered brother, by contrast, "earned forgiveness for his sins and was admitted into Paradise."

**A debt that never closes.** Imam Ahmad recorded from ʿAbdullah bin Masʿud that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Any soul that is unjustly killed, then the first son of Adam will carry a burden of its shedding, for he was the first to practice the crime of murder." Ibn Kathir notes this hadith was also recorded by the Group with the exception of Abu Dawud. And Ibn Jarir recorded that ʿAbdullah bin ʿAmr used to say that this son of Adam "will be the most miserable among men," carrying a share of every drop of blood shed on earth until the Day of Resurrection, "for he was the first person to establish murder." Ibn Kathir also brings a hadith of the Prophet ﷺ warning that no sin is more deserving of Allah hastening its punishment in this world — on top of what is stored up in the Hereafter — than transgression and cutting the ties of the womb; and Qabil's act, he observes, combined both.

## Ayah 31 — the crow, and the first burial

Qabil now stood over the first corpse in history with no idea what to do with it. So Allah sent a teacher — a crow, *yabḥathu fī al-arḍ*, scratching and digging in the ground, "to show him how to hide the dead body of his brother." As-Suddi relates from the Companions that Allah sent two crows which fought until one killed the other; the survivor then dug a hole, placed the dead bird in it, and threw earth over it — acting out before Qabil's eyes both his own crime and its remedy. Ibn ʿAbbas's narration (via ʿAli bin Abi Talhah) is similar: a crow came to a dead crow and covered it with earth until it was hidden.

The man who had thought himself clever enough to take a life was outdone by a bird: "Woe to me! Am I not even able to be as this crow and to hide the dead body of my brother?" So mankind learned burial — the dignified concealment of the dead — not from human wisdom but from a lesson Allah staged through one of His smallest creatures.

*Fa-aṣbaḥa min al-nādimīn* — "then he became one of those who regretted." Al-Hasan al-Basri's comment is quietly devastating: "Allah made him feel sorrow after the loss that he earned." His regret was itself part of his punishment — grief arriving only after the loss was sealed.

## Ayah 32 — one life is all life

Now the Qur'an lifts its eyes from the two brothers to all of humanity. *Min ajli dhālik* — "because of that," says Ibn Kathir, because the son of Adam killed his brother in transgression and aggression — "We ordained for the Children of Israel that whoever kills a soul, except in retaliation for murder or for spreading corruption in the land, it is as if he had killed all mankind; and whoever saves one, it is as if he had saved all mankind."

Ibn Kathir gives the reason in a single phrase: "because there is no difference between one life and another." Human life is not a quantity that can be discounted; each soul carries the full sanctity of the species. The early authorities turned the jewel to show its facets. Ibn ʿAbbas said: whoever kills one soul that Allah has forbidden is just like one who kills all mankind. Mujahid explained that whoever kills a believing soul intentionally faces Allah's Fire, His anger, His curse and a tremendous punishment — "equal to if he had killed all people, his punishment will still be the same." And the saving of life? Ibn ʿAbbas and Mujahid explained that "saving" here occurs by *refraining* — whoever forbids himself the shedding of blood has, in effect, given all mankind their lives, for every person on earth is safe from him. Saʿid bin Jubayr put it in balance: "He who allows himself to shed the blood of a Muslim is like he who allows shedding the blood of all people. He who forbids shedding the blood of one Muslim is like he who forbids shedding the blood of all people."

**A Companion who lived this ayah.** Ibn Kathir preserves an unforgettable scene. When ʿUthman ؓ was besieged in his house, Abu Hurayrah came to him and said, "I came to give you my support. Now it is good to fight, O Leader of the Faithful!" ʿUthman answered: "O Abu Hurayrah! Does it please you that you kill all people, including me?" He said, "No." ʿUthman said: "If you kill one man, it is as if you killed all people." So Abu Hurayrah turned back and did not fight. The Caliph of the Muslims, facing his own murderers, applied this ayah against the drawing of a sword in his own defense.

The ayah ends on a sorrowful note: "And indeed Our Messengers came to them with clear proofs (al-bayyināt), yet even after that many of them continued to exceed the limits in the land." Ibn Kathir explains that this chastises those who violate what they know to be forbidden, and he points to the Jewish tribes of Madinah — Qurayzah, al-Nadir and Qaynuqaʿ — who in the days before Islam would fight alongside Aws or Khazraj against their own people, then ransom the captives and pay blood money afterward, believing in part of the Scripture and rejecting part, as Surat al-Baqarah (2:84–85) condemns.

## Why this story is told here

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws attention to the placement. The preceding passage described how the Children of Israel cowered when commanded to fight in Allah's cause; this story is set against it as the opposite extreme — unjust killing. The Qur'an is teaching balance: it is an error to shrink from fighting to uphold truth, and equally a "stock destruction of one's material and spiritual life, both in the present world and in the Hereafter," to kill and fight unjustly. Cowardice before a just cause and aggression without one are two failures of the same scale.

## Living it

**When wronged, be Habil.** Imam Ahmad recorded that at the onset of the fitnah (civil strife) surrounding ʿUthman, Saʿd bin Abi Waqqas bore witness that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "There will be a fitnah; he who sits idle during it is better than he who stands up, and he who stands up is better than he who walks, and he who walks is better than he who runs." Asked, "What if someone enters my home and stretches his hand to kill me?" he ﷺ said: "Be just like the son of Adam." At-Tirmidhi also recorded this and graded it Hasan. And in the hadith of the Two Sahihs: "When two Muslims meet each other with their swords, both the murderer and the murdered will go to the Hellfire" — the victim too, "for he surely had the intention to kill his comrade." In blind strife between believers, the one who refuses to raise his hand, as Habil refused, is the one who escapes with his Hereafter intact.

**The cure for envy.** The crime began with hasad — envy at a blessing Allah gave another. The remedy, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān relates (citing Mazhari), is to read one's own deprivation as the result of one's own shortcomings and turn to repentance and self-correction — not to scheme for the other person to lose what Allah gave him, for that brings the envier nothing but loss: acceptability with Allah depends on taqwa alone.

**And guard the deed behind the deed.** The root of it all was a rejected sacrifice, and the principle Habil spoke — "Allah accepts only from those who have taqwa" — weighed heavily on the righteous of the early generations. ʿAmir ibn ʿAbdullah wept on his deathbed, and when asked why a man of lifelong worship should weep, he answered that this very ayah was ringing in his ears — he did not know whether any worship of his had been accepted. Abu al-Darda' said that to know Allah had accepted a single prayer of his would be better to him than the world and all it contains; Ibn Masʿud said he would not surrender the certainty of one accepted deed even if the whole world were turned to solid gold and passed into his possession; and ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAziz wrote, "Hold on to taqwa, without which no deed is accepted... There are many who preach it but very few who practice it."

The passage closes the first chapter of human history with its two enduring figures: the brother who feared Allah and would not kill, and the brother who let his soul make murder look fair — and with Allah's own accounting of what one life is worth: everything.

passages.title: The penalty for waging war on society
passages.tafsir:
These two ayat lay down the Qur'an's penalty for what the jurists call *muḥārabah* — "waging war against Allah and His Messenger" by armed assault on public peace — and then, remarkably, throw open a door of escape: whoever repents before he is captured is spared the punishment altogether. Severity and mercy are deliberately paired, and neither can be understood without the other.

## Why this follows the story of Habil

Ayat 27–32 told of the first murder, when the son of Adam killed his brother, and ended with the ordinance given to the Children of Israel: whoever kills one soul unjustly, it is as if he killed all mankind, and whoever saves one, it is as if he saved all mankind. Ibn Kathir explains that killing without justification is this grave "because there is no difference between one life and another" — and that "saving a life" means holding its blood sacred, so that "whoever forbids killing a soul without justification, the lives of all people will be saved from him" (Ibn 'Abbas). Sa'id bin Jubayr put it starkly, in two mirrored halves: he who allows himself to shed the blood of a Muslim is like he who allows shedding the blood of all people, and he who forbids shedding the blood of one Muslim is like he who forbids shedding the blood of all people. Ibn Kathir even records 'Uthman, besieged in his own house, turning away Abu Hurayrah's offer to fight in his defence with the words: "If you kill one man, it is as if you killed all people."

Ayah 32 then closed with a rebuke: the Messengers came with clear proofs, "even then after that many of them continued to exceed the limits in the land." Ayah 33 answers that excess. Having established how sacred a single life is, the passage now legislates against those who assault life, property and public safety wholesale.

## What "waging war against Allah and His Messenger" means

The key word is *yuḥāribūna*, from *ḥarb* (war). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that *ḥarb* intrinsically means to wrest or snatch away, and stands opposite *salm* — peace and security. So *muḥārabah* is not any fight; it is the destruction of public peace itself. The commentary distinguishes it from *muqātalah*, ordinary combat: *muḥārabah* denotes high-handed, organised, armed assault on people's lives, property and honour — highway robbery, brigandage, rebellion. Hence the jurists (as in Tafsir Mazhari) hold that this ayah targets a group or individual who robs people and breaks the law of the land by force of arms — not common thieves and pickpockets, whose rare offences do not shatter public security.

And why is it called war "against Allah and His Messenger," when the victims are ordinary people? Ibn Kathir says "wage war" here means to oppose and contradict — including disbelief, blocking the roads, and spreading fear in the fairways. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds the deeper point: when a powerful group elects to break by force the Law given by Allah and His Messenger, it is really at war with the government — and when that government is one which upholds and enforces the Law of Allah and His Messenger, their fighting is rightly counted as fighting *against* Allah and His Messenger, even though their aggression visibly falls on ordinary human beings.

## The four penalties in ayah 33

The ayah names four: that they be killed, or crucified, or their hands and feet cut off on opposite sides, or exiled from the land. The scholars differed over the word *aw* ("or"):

- **Choice.** Ibn 'Abbas said the Muslim leader may choose among the punishments for one who takes up arms and spreads fear on the roads — the view of Sa'id bin Al-Musayyib, Mujahid, 'Ata', Al-Hasan Al-Basri, Ibrahim An-Nakha'i and Ad-Dahhak, and among the four Imams, Malik. Ibn Kathir supports this by parallel ayat (5:95 and the expiation verses) where *aw* plainly offers options.
- **Gradation by crime.** Abu Hanifah, Al-Shafi'i and Ahmad, with a group of Companions and Successors, read *aw* as assigning each penalty to a different case. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites a report from Ibn 'Abbas: after Abu Burdah Aslami broke his treaty with the Prophet ﷺ and robbed people travelling to Madinah to embrace Islam, Jibra'il brought the injunction that whoever killed and looted is crucified; whoever killed only is killed; whoever looted only has hand and foot cut on opposite sides; and whoever neither killed nor plundered but frightened the people of the roads is exiled.

On exile (*yunfaw min al-arḍ*), Ibn Kathir records several understandings: that the fugitive is pursued until captured or driven from the land of Islam (Ibn 'Abbas, Anas, Malik and others); that he is expelled to another town within Muslim lands (Sa'id bin Jubayr, Az-Zuhri and others); or that he is imprisoned. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān relates 'Umar's verdict here: expelling such a man just exports his menace to another city — so lock him in prison; that is his "removal from the land." Abu Hanifah adopted this view.

**Whom was it revealed about?** Ibn Jarir records from 'Ikrimah and Al-Hasan Al-Basri — and Abu Dawud and An-Nasa'i record from Ibn 'Abbas — that the ayat came down concerning the idolators. But Ibn Kathir rules that the correct opinion is that the ayah is general, covering everyone who commits these crimes. He cites the incident behind it, recorded by Al-Bukhari and Muslim from Anas bin Malik: eight men of the 'Ukl (or 'Uraynah) tribe pledged Islam, fell ill in Madinah's climate, and were sent by the Prophet ﷺ to recover among the milk-camels. Once healthy, they killed the shepherd and drove off the herd. They were pursued, captured, and punished with amputation and death — treachery, murder and plunder answered with the full weight of this ayah.

## Hadd, not ordinary punishment

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān frames the whole passage within the Shari'ah's three kinds of penalty. *Ḥudūd* (singular *ḥadd*) are punishments fixed by Allah as His own right (*ḥaqq Allāh*): no ruler may alter, reduce or pardon them, and no intercession in them is permitted. *Qiṣāṣ* (even retaliation) is fixed but held as the right of the victim's heirs, who may exact it or forgive. *Taʿzīrāt* are discretionary penalties left to the judge. Only five ḥudūd exist: for robbery, theft, adultery, false accusation of adultery, and — by consensus of the Companions — wine-drinking. And the ḥudūd carry a famous protection: *al-ḥudūd tundraʾu bi'sh-shubuhāt* — they are dropped where there is doubt; the strictest punishments demand the strictest proof, with taʿzīr filling the gap when proof falls short.

The penalty of ayah 33 is a ḥadd, and the Arabic itself signals it. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān observes that the first three verbs (*yuqattalū, yuṣallabū, tuqaṭṭaʿa*) come in an emphatic, intensive form (*bāb al-tafʿīl*) with plural objects — hinting, first, that the whole armed band shares liability even if one member did the killing (each acted trusting in the others' backing), and second, that this is not qiṣāṣ: even if the victims' families forgive, the penalty stands, for the right violated is Allah's. The crime is against society's very security, so no private party can waive it.

Why such severity? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān answers that the Qur'an, unlike worldly penal codes, never legislates punishment in isolation: it welds each penalty to the fear of Allah and the Hereafter, and it is this — not police or armies — that actually uproots crime from a society.

## "Disgrace in this world, and a great torment in the Hereafter"

The close of ayah 33 stacks two punishments: public disgrace now — "shame, humiliation, punishment, contempt," in Ibn Jarir's words — and a tremendous torment later. Ibn Kathir explains that the threat of the Hereafter falls on those who die unrepentant. For the believer, the worldly penalty can itself purify: Muslim records in his Sahih from 'Ubadah bin As-Samit that the Prophet ﷺ took the pledge that whoever falls into sin and is punished for it, that punishment is his expiation; and whoever Allah screens, his matter rests with Allah — to punish or pardon. 'Ali narrated that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said that Allah is far more just than to punish a servant twice for a sin already punished in this life, and far more generous than to revisit what He has already pardoned — recorded by Ahmad, Ibn Majah and At-Tirmidhi, who graded it Hasan Gharib; Ad-Daraqutni held the narration from the Prophet ﷺ to be Sahih. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds the converse caution: worldly punishment does not automatically clear the account of the Hereafter — that requires genuine tawbah (repentance).

## Ayah 34: the door left open

"Except those who repent before you overpower them — then know that Allah is Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful." If the brigand abandons his crime *while still at large*, before the authorities seize him, the entire ḥadd — killing, crucifixion, amputation — is waived. Ibn Kathir notes this was the practice of the Companions, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān stresses how exceptional it is: in every other ḥadd (theft, adultery), repentance may clear the Hereafter but never lifts the worldly penalty. Only robbery carries this exception — and only for repentance *before* arrest; repentance after arrest does not lift the worldly sentence.

The commentary draws out the wisdom. The penalty is uniquely severe — a whole band may be executed for one member's act — so the law is made correspondingly soft at its edge. There is also a practical mercy: an armed group is hard to overpower, so the door of persuasion is kept open; and since Islam wants killing to be as rare as possible, reform is pursued alongside deterrence.

The sources show it working. 'Ali al-Asadi robbed the roads and shed blood, and no force could capture him — until he heard a man reciting, "O My servants who have transgressed against themselves! Despair not of the mercy of Allah; verily, Allah forgives all sins" (39:53). He asked to hear it again, sheathed his sword, and came to Madinah in repentance. Abu Hurayrah took his hand and testified for him before the governor Marwan bin Al-Hakam — "he came in repentance and you do not have a way against him, nor can you have him killed" — and al-Asadi lived out his repentance, dying at sea on campaign against the Romans. Likewise Harithah bin Badr At-Tamimi, who had spread mischief around Basrah: 'Ali refused the intercessors who first approached him, but when Sa'id bin Qays asked him about the ayah and 'Ali recited it through "except those who repent before you overpower them," 'Ali wrote him a document of safety.

Ibn Jarir also preserves a sobering counter-example: a man of Murad came to Abu Musa in Kufah declaring his repentance before capture, and was left in peace — but later rose again against the authorities, "and Allah punished him for his sins and he was killed." Amnesty is real, but it is not a game.

**What repentance does not erase.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is emphatic: the waiver cancels the ḥadd — Allah's right — not the rights of His servants. Stolen property still in hand must be returned; destroyed wealth must be compensated or forgiven by its owner; and if anyone was killed or wounded, the law of qiṣāṣ still applies, forgivable only by the victim's heirs. This is the position of Abu Hanifah and the majority — and it is really the definition of sincere tawbah itself: repentance that keeps the loot is no repentance at all.

Read whole, the passage is a portrait of divine justice: a society in which one life weighs as heavy as all mankind's must defend its peace with terrible seriousness — yet even the highway robber, sword still in hand, is met on the road by "Despair not of the mercy of Allah."

passages.title: Seeking nearness to Allah versus the ransomless Fire
passages.tafsir:
# Seeking Nearness to Allah versus the Ransomless Fire (5:35–37)

This short passage sets two destinies side by side. In ayah 35 the believers are given three commands — fear Allah, seek the *wasilah* (means of nearness) to Him, and strive in His way — with success as the promised outcome. In ayat 36–37 the opposite picture is painted: those who disbelieve will find, on the Day of Resurrection, that no ransom can buy them out of the torment and no exit from the Fire will ever open. What binds the three ayat together is a single question: what actually brings a person close to Allah — and what happens to the one who never sought that closeness at all.

## Why these ayat sit in the middle of laws of punishment

The placement is deliberate. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out that the verses just before this passage laid down the prescribed punishment for robbery and rebellion, and the punishment for theft follows only three verses later. In between, the Qurʼān pauses to speak of taqwa, obedience, striving in Allah's way, and the ruin of disbelief. This, Maʿārif observes, is the Qurʼān's recurring style: it does not merely state the letter of a penal law as a cold, coercive command and leave it there. Like an affectionate nurturer, it works on the heart itself — awakening the fear of Allah and the reality of the Hereafter, bringing the everlasting bliss of Paradise almost within sight — so that the taste for crime is replaced by distaste for it. The law restrains the hand; these ayat aim to change the heart, for as Maʿārif says, it is the fear of Allah alone that can really stop a person from sinning both openly and in secret.

## Three commands in ayah 35

**First: taqwa.** Ibn Kathir notes a precise point of usage: when taqwa (mindfulness, fear of Allah) is mentioned alongside commands of obedience, it specifically means refraining from the prohibitions and forbidden matters. So the ayah's structure is: keep away from what Allah has forbidden, then actively seek what draws you to Him.

**Second: seek the wasilah to Him.** This is the heart of the ayah, opened up below.

**Third: strive in His cause.** After commanding avoidance of the prohibited and the pursuit of obedience, Allah commands the believers to strive against His enemies, and encourages them with what He has prepared for the Day of Resurrection — Ibn Kathir describes the lofty, safe and beautiful dwellings of Paradise whose people will always be comfortable and never miserable, living and never dying, their clothes never growing thin and their youth never ending.

Maʿārif adds two subtleties about why jihad is named separately here. Striving in Allah's way is already included in "good deeds," but it is singled out to mark its rank — the Prophet ﷺ said that jihad is the highest peak of Islam. And there is a second wisdom tied to context: ayat 32–33 had just condemned *fasād fī al-arḍ*, spreading disorder on the earth. On a surface view, an ignorant person might confuse fighting with disorder. So the Qurʼān first forbade corruption, then commanded jihad with the qualifying words *fī sabīlihi* — "in His way." Robbery and rebellion kill and plunder for personal aggrandizement; striving in Allah's way is for upholding the Word of Allah and eliminating oppression and tyranny. As Maʿārif puts it, there is a world of difference between the two.

## The word "wasilah": nearness sought with longing and love

The command *wabtaghū ilayhi al-wasīlah* — "seek the means of approach to Him" — turns on one rich Arabic word. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, drawing on the lexicons (the Ṣiḥāḥ of Jauhari, the Mufradāt of Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī, Lisān al-ʿArab), explains that *wasilah* derives from a verbal noun meaning to make an effort to become close to someone. Arabic has a near-twin of this word spelled with the letter ṣād, which means closeness in the absolute sense — any kind of nearness or joining. But *wasilah* spelled with sīn, the word used here, carries something more: it means seeking to gain nearness **with longing and love**. The ayah is not asking for mechanical proximity; it is asking the believer to close the distance to his Lord the way a lover closes distance — deliberately, yearningly.

What, concretely, is this means of approach? The earliest authorities answer with one voice. Ibn Kathir records the chain: Sufyan ath-Thawri said that Talhah said that ʿAtaʼ said that **Ibn ʿAbbas** said that wasilah means "the means of approach" — and Mujahid, Abu Waʼil, Al-Hasan, Qatadah, ʿAbdullah bin Kathir, As-Suddi, Ibn Zayd and others gave the same meaning. **Qatadah** put it most practically: "Seek the means of approach to Him by obeying Him and performing the acts that please Him." Maʿārif adds that Hudhayfah (as reported by Hakim) said wasilah means nearness and obedience, and Ibn Jarir reported the same from ʿAtaʼ, Mujahid and Hasan al-Basri. The gist, as Maʿārif summarises: seek the nearness of Allah through īmān (faith) and righteous deeds. Ibn Kathir notes the Qurʼān uses the word in exactly this sense elsewhere: "Those whom they call upon seek a means of access to their Lord" (17:57).

## The Wasilah that belongs to the Prophet ﷺ

The word has a second, wondrous usage. Ibn Kathir explains that *al-Wasilah* is also the name of the highest grade in Paradise — the residence of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, the grade nearest to Allah's Throne. Two hadith in the bundle establish this:

- **Al-Bukhari** recorded from Jabir bin ʿAbdullah that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: whoever, on hearing the adhan, says, "O Allah! Lord of this perfect call and of the regular prayer which is going to be established! Grant Muhammad the Wasilah and superiority, and send him to the praiseworthy station which You have promised him" — intercession from the Prophet ﷺ will be permitted for him on the Day of Resurrection.
- **Muslim** recorded from ʿAbdullah bin ʿAmr bin al-ʿĀṣ that the Prophet ﷺ said: when you hear the muʼadhdhin, repeat what he says, then ask Allah to send blessings on me — whoever asks one blessing for me, Allah grants him ten — then ask for the Wasilah for me, "for it is a grade in Paradise that only one servant of Allah deserves, and I hope that I am that servant. Whoever asks Allah for the Wasilah for me will earn the right of my intercession."

Maʿārif also cites a sound (sahih) hadith in the **Musnad of Ahmad** in which the Prophet ﷺ said that the Wasilah is a high rank of Paradise above which there is no rank, and instructed his community to pray that Allah give it to him.

An obvious question follows: if that supreme Wasilah is the Prophet's ﷺ alone, how can every believer be commanded to "seek the wasilah"? Maʿārif answers: just as the highest station of guidance is special to the Prophet ﷺ while its elementary and intermediate ranks are open to all Muslims, so the highest rank of nearness is his alone, and all the ranks beneath it are open to every believer — through the linkage of their love for him.

## Love, the Sunnah, and how the ranks are climbed

That word "love" is not incidental. Maʿārif reports that Mujaddid Alf-Thani (in his Letters) and Qadi Thanaʼullah of Panipat (in Tafsir Mazhari) both drew attention to the longing and love embedded in the very word wasilah: advancement in the ranks of nearness depends on love for Allah and His Messenger ﷺ — and love comes through following the Sunnah, for Allah says: "If you do love Allah, follow me; Allah shall love you" (3:31). The more faithfully one follows the Prophet's ﷺ example — in worship, transactions, dealings, morals, social life, every department of living — the more beloved of Allah one becomes, and the closer and nearer to Him.

Maʿārif then draws a further conclusion of its own. Since everything that earns Allah's pleasure is a wasilah to Him, this includes not only faith and good deeds but also the company and love of the prophets and the righteous, for that too is among the causes of Allah's pleasure. On this basis Maʿārif judges — in its own careful wording — that praying to Allah by making them a wasilah "should be correct," and it supports this with the report that ʿUmar, at a time of famine, made ʿAbbas a wasilah in his prayer for rain before Allah, and the prayer was answered. Maʿārif also reports (citing Manār) that the Prophet ﷺ himself taught a blind Companion to pray with these words: "O Allah, I seek from You, and I ask for Your attention with (the Wasilah of) Your Prophet, Muhammad, the Prophet of Mercy."

## Ayat 36–37: the ransom that will never be accepted

Then the camera turns. Against the believer seeking nearness stands the disbeliever on the Day of Resurrection, offering wealth for distance — distance from the torment. Ayah 36 states the offer at its logical extreme: if a disbeliever owned everything on earth, *and as much again with it*, and offered all of it to ransom himself from the punishment, it would never be accepted. Ibn Kathir paints the scene: the earth's fill of gold and twice that amount, offered by a man who sees the torment surrounding him and is certain he will suffer it — refused. There is no evading it and no buying out of it. "And theirs would be a painful torment."

Maʿārif reads these two ayat as a diagnosis of the sinner's whole economy. Most sin, it observes, is committed for personal desires or for family — and since fulfilling desires takes wealth, people chase acquisition without distinguishing halal from haram. The ayah censures this acquisition mania as ultimately futile: the race for more never ends in this life ("more and more stays to be the order of every other day"), and when the punishment of the Last Day comes into view, the entire hoard — even doubled — buys nothing. A little honest reflection on this, Maʿārif says, could bring an instant revolution in a person's life.

Ayah 37 then closes the last door: "They will long to get out of the Fire, but never will they get out therefrom; and theirs will be a lasting torment." Ibn Kathir links it to Allah's words elsewhere: "Every time they seek to get away therefrom, in anguish, they will be driven back therein." The severity of the pain keeps the longing to escape alive forever, yet escape never comes — the more the flames lift them toward the upper part of Hell, the more the angels of punishment strike them with iron bars and they fall back to its depths. The "lasting torment" (*ʿadhāb muqīm*) means, in Ibn Kathir's words, eternal and everlasting.

The bundle records one hadith that turns ayah 36 into a dialogue. Anas bin Malik narrated that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: a man from the people of the Fire will be brought forth and asked, "O son of Adam! How did you find your dwelling?" He will say, "The worst dwelling." He will be asked, "Would you ransom yourself with the earth's fill of gold?" He will say, "Yes, O Lord!" Allah will say, "You have lied. I asked you for what is less than that and you did not do it" — and he will be ordered to the Fire. Muslim and An-Nasaʼi recorded it. The hadith exposes the terrible irony of ayah 36: the man now willing to pay a planet of gold was once unwilling to pay something far smaller — faith and obedience while the offer still stood.

## Living the passage

The passage leaves the believer with a clear program, drawn straight from its three commands. Keep away from what Allah has forbidden — that is the taqwa this ayah intends. Then actively seek nearness: not as a vague mood but through the concrete means the Salaf named — obedience, faith, and deeds that please Allah — pursued, as the word wasilah itself demands, with longing and love, and climbed rank by rank through following the Sunnah of the Prophet ﷺ. Add to that the duas the Prophet ﷺ himself taught after the adhan, which join the believer's daily routine to his ﷺ Wasilah and to his intercession. And hold ayat 36–37 in view whenever the pull of unlawful gain appears: everything that can be amassed in this world, doubled, will not buy one moment's relief on that Day — while what Allah actually asks for is less than that, and it is asked for now.

passages.title: The theft penalty, repentance, and divine sovereignty
passages.tafsir:
# The Theft Penalty, Repentance, and Divine Sovereignty (5:38–40)

This short passage lays down the prescribed punishment (hadd) for theft, immediately opens the door of repentance to the one who committed it, and then lifts the reader's gaze to the sovereignty of Allah over the heavens and the earth — the Master whose right it is both to punish and to forgive. The three ayat form one movement: law (ayah 38), mercy (ayah 39), and the divine authority that grounds them both (ayah 40).

## Why both "the male thief and the female thief"?

Ayah 38 opens: *"As for the male thief and the female thief, cut off their hands…"* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws attention to something easy to miss. In Qur'anic legislation generally — prayer, fasting, Hajj, zakah — the address is to men, and women are understood to be included by implication. But here, as in the verse of adultery, both sexes are named separately and explicitly. Why? Because this is a matter of hudud — the fixed punishments of the Shariʿah — and in hudud the least doubt causes the punishment to be dropped. Women were therefore not left as merely implied; they were spelled out, so that no room for doubt could arise.

Maʿārif notes a further subtlety: in the theft verse the man is mentioned first, while in the adultery verse (24:2) the woman comes first. Commentators offered several explanations for this reversal; the one the author finds most compelling is that theft is a graver lapse in a man, because Allah has given him strength and open avenues to earn his living — for him to stoop to theft despite that deepens the disgrace. In adultery, by contrast, Allah has endowed woman with natural modesty and a protected environment, so her fall into that crime is the graver one. Each verse fronts the party whose guilt is weightier.

## "A recompense… a deterrent from Allah": what the closing words teach

Two phrases follow the command, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān unpacks both.

**Jazāʼan bimā kasabā** — "a recompense for what they earned." Ibn Kathir adds a pointed observation on the fittingness of the penalty: they stole people's property *with their hands*, so it is fitting that the very tool of the crime be cut off as punishment from Allah for their error.

**Nakālan min Allāh** — "a deterrent from Allah." The Arabic word *nakāl* means an exemplary punishment: one that not only punishes the offender but teaches a lesson to onlookers, so that they too abandon any intention of crime. Any translation must carry both senses — lesson and dissuasion. The aim, in Maʿārif's phrase, is to punish one and chasten the rest, so that this ugly crime is eradicated altogether.

The words *min Allāh* ("from Allah") carry a legal weight of their own. Maʿārif explains that theft can be viewed two ways: as an injustice against the victim, and as a violation of Allah's command. If the punishment were merely the victim's right — as in qisas (even retaliation) — the victim's pardon would cancel it. But by attaching the punishment to Allah, the verse marks it as a *hadd*: a Right of Allah (Haqqullah), fixed by the Qur'an itself and not left to any authority's discretion. In a manner of speaking, it is a crime against the State — so even if the person robbed forgives the thief, the punishment does not lapse.

Finally, the verse closes: *"And Allah is Mighty, Wise."* Maʿārif reads this as the answer to the objection — loudly made in modern times — that this punishment is harsh, even "savage." The pairing of the two names tells us that the severity of the penalty flows not from raw power alone but from wisdom. Ibn Kathir reads the pair similarly: All-Powerful in His punishment, All-Wise in what He commands, forbids, legislates, and decrees.

## Not every theft is *sariqah*: the strict conditions of the hadd

Both commentaries stress that this punishment is hedged with conditions. Ibn Kathir notes that cutting the thief's hand was already the practice in the time of Jahiliyyah; Islam upheld it — but attached to it several conditions that must be met before it is carried out.

**The minimum value.** Ibn Kathir cites the hadith recorded in the Two Sahihs from Abu Hurayrah, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: *"May Allah curse the thief who steals an egg and as a result his hand is cut off, and who steals rope and as a result his hand is cut off."* Al-Bukhari and Muslim record from ʿA'ishah that he ﷺ said: *"The hand of the thief shall be cut off if he steals a quarter of a Dinar or more,"* and Muslim records her narration: *"The hand of the thief shall only be cut off if he steals a quarter of a Dinar or more."* Ibn Kathir calls this hadith the basis of the matter, fixing the threshold at a quarter dinar. The reported view that it is three dirhams is no contradiction, since the dinar then equalled twelve dirhams — three dirhams *is* a quarter dinar. This position is reported from ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, ʿUthman, and ʿAli, and held by ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAziz, al-Layth ibn Saʿd, al-Awzaʿi, ash-Shafiʿi and his companions, Ahmad ibn Hanbal, Ishaq ibn Rahwayh (in one narration), Abu Thawr, and Dawud az-Zahiri. Abu Hanifah and his students Abu Yusuf, Muhammad, and Zufar, along with Sufyan ath-Thawri, held the minimum to be ten dirhams. Ibn Kathir judges the first view correct, and remarks on its wisdom: so low a threshold was set precisely so that people would refrain from theft altogether.

**The definition of the crime.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, citing the lexicon Al-Qāmūs, defines *sariqah* — in language and in law — as taking another's property from a secured place, without permission, clandestinely. Four ingredients must all be present:

1. **Privately owned** — the thief must own no share in it, with no doubt of ownership, and it must not be public-welfare property in which all people share.
2. **Secured** — kept in a locked house or under guard; even a doubt about its being secured drops the hadd.
3. **Without permission** — one given access to the property who then takes it is not liable to the hadd; a mere doubt of permission drops it.
4. **Taken by stealth** — open seizure is robbery, not theft, and carries its own already-stated punishment.

Maʿārif then works through the practical consequences, drawing (as it states) on the authoritative Hanafi work *Badā'iʿ al-Sanā'iʿ*: theft from public places like a mosque, park, station, train, or airplane; stealing fruit from trees or honey; a servant, worker, friend, or relative who was allowed into the house and takes something; pickpocketing, snatching, fraud, or breach of trust; the stealer of coffin-cloths; theft from jointly owned property in which the thief has a share — in none of these is the hand cut. And the law of evidence for hudud is deliberately stricter than for ordinary matters: the testimony of two men is required, whereas common cases may be judged on the evidence of one man and two women; a sinner's testimony is inadmissible, even though in other matters a judge has the option to accept it if satisfied that the person does not lie; and delayed testimony — a month or more after the event — is not accepted.

Two clarifications matter here. First, where the hadd is dropped, the culprit does not walk free: the ruling authority may impose discretionary punishment (*taʿzir*), which can be physical, such as lashes. Second, the absence of the hadd never makes the act lawful — property taken without its owner's consent remains haram and brings punishment in the Hereafter, as the verse says: *"And do not eat up each other's property by false means"* (2:188).

The upshot, as Maʿārif puts it, is that the Shariʿah has done two things at once: fixed a stern penalty, and hedged its enforcement with extreme precaution — the standing rule being that the benefit of doubt goes to the accused. The occasion for actually enforcing the hadd arises only rarely; yet its standing awe deters crime so effectively that, in lands where these punishments are applied, one sees neither crowds of amputees nor waves of theft. Maʿārif points to what pilgrims themselves witness in Saudi Arabia: shops full of merchandise left open at every prayer time, their owners returning from the mosque in perfect peace. Mercy shown to the professional criminal, the author observes, amounts to tyranny against the whole of harassed humanity.

## Ayah 39: which repentance lifts which punishment?

*"But whoever repents after his wrongdoing and does righteous good deeds, then verily, Allah will pardon him. Verily, Allah is Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful."*

Ibn Kathir states the plain sense: whoever repents and returns to Allah after committing theft, Allah forgives him. But Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws a precise legal distinction by comparing this verse with the robbery passage a few verses earlier. There, Allah made an explicit exception: *"except those who repent before you overpower them"* (5:34) — so the robber who repents before arrest is exempted from the temporal hadd itself. Here, no such exemption appears. The wording *"then Allah shall relent towards him"* indicates that this repentance operates in terms of the Hereafter: the ruler does not drop the hadd because of it, but Allah, by forgiving the crime, grants the penitent deliverance from the punishment of the next life. On this basis, Maʿārif reports, the Muslim jurists agree almost unanimously: the repentant robber (before capture) escapes the hadd; the repentant thief — whether he repents before or after arrest — does not escape the temporal punishment, though his sin is forgiven and his Hereafter secured.

## The woman of Makhzum: the story behind the verse

Ibn Kathir relates the occasion that brings ayat 38–39 to life. Imam Ahmad recorded from ʿAbdullah bin ʿAmr that a woman stole during the time of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. Her victims brought her forward; her people offered ransom — even five hundred dinars — and twice he ﷺ answered only: *"Cut off her hand."* When it was done, the woman asked, "O Messenger of Allah! Is there a chance for me to repent?" He said: *"Yes. This day, you are free from your sin just as the day your mother gave birth to you."* And Allah sent down ayah 39.

Her story is also narrated in the Two Sahihs, from Az-Zuhri, from ʿUrwah, from ʿA'ishah. She was a woman of the tribe of Makhzum who stole at the time of the Conquest of Makkah, and her case alarmed the Quraysh. Who would dare intercede? Only Usamah bin Zayd, the Prophet's ﷺ beloved. When Usamah spoke to him, the face of the Messenger ﷺ changed colour with anger: *"Do you intercede in a punishment prescribed by Allah?"* Usamah begged him to seek forgiveness for him. That night the Prophet ﷺ stood, praised Allah, and declared: *"Those who were before you were destroyed because when an honorable person among them would steal, they would leave him. But when a weak man among them stole, they implemented the prescribed punishment against him. By Him in Whose Hand is my soul! If Fatimah the daughter of Muhammad stole, I will have her hand cut off."*

The story does not end with the sentence. In Muslim's wording, ʿA'ishah said: "Her repentance was sincere afterwards, and she got married, and she used to come to me so that I convey her needs to the Messenger of Allah." The two halves of the passage meet in one life: the hadd applied without favour to rank or ransom, and a repentance so fully accepted that its bearer became a welcome visitor in the Prophet's ﷺ own household. Equality before the law of Allah, and no despair after it.

## Ayah 40: the Master's right to punish and to forgive

*"Do you not know that to Allah alone belongs the kingdom of the heavens and the earth? He punishes whom He wills and He forgives whom He wills. And Allah is powerful over everything."*

Why close a passage of criminal law with a declaration of cosmic sovereignty? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān answers: a shallow look at these stringent injunctions could give the false impression that they contradict human dignity. To remove that doubt, Allah states first that He alone is the real Master of the entire universe, and last that He is the Absolute Power — and in between, that He does not only punish; He forgives as well. Both forgiveness and punishment rest on His Wisdom: as He is Absolute Master and Absolute Power, so is He Absolutely Wise. No human power can gauge the extent of His dominion, and no human reason can fully fathom the manifestations of His Wisdom — yet what reflection does yield is enough to set the heart at peace. Ibn Kathir's comment is of the same breath: He owns everything, decides what He wills for it, and no one can resist His judgment.

## Living it

The passage trains the believer in three directions at once. Toward property: the sanctity of other people's wealth is so weighty that even a quarter dinar, taken by stealth from its secured place, forfeits the hand that took it — and what escapes the earthly court remains haram before Allah. Toward justice: no rank, wealth, or beloved intercessor bends the hudud of Allah — the nations before us perished precisely by sparing their nobles and punishing their weak. And toward mercy: no sin, once punished or unpunished, closes the door of tawbah; the thief who repents and mends her ways can stand before Allah as clean, in the Prophet's ﷺ words, as the day her mother gave birth to her. Law without mercy hardens; mercy without law dissolves; ayah 40 holds them together in the hand of the One to whom the kingdom of the heavens and the earth belongs.

passages.title: Those who race to disbelief seek the Prophet's judgment
passages.tafsir:
This passage is Allah's consolation to His Messenger ﷺ over a wound that cut deep: people were coming to his court not to seek truth, but to shop for a verdict. Ayah 41 names the players — hypocrites who profess faith with their mouths while their hearts are empty, and Jews of Madinah's environs who listen eagerly to lies — and comforts the Prophet ﷺ: "do not grieve." Ayah 42 then gives him his instructions as judge, and ayah 43 delivers the devastating question that exposes the whole game: why would they seek your ruling when the Tawrah, containing Allah's own judgment, sits in their hands? What binds the three ayat together is a single drama — the manipulation of Allah's law by people who knew better — and the standard of pure justice Allah sets against it.

## Two disputes behind the revelation

The commentators preserve two occasions for these ayat, and Ibn Kathir concludes that "both of these were the reasons behind revealing these Ayat, and Allah knows best."

**The blood-money case.** Ibn Kathir records this occasion through more than one narration, and the details differ between them, so they are best kept side by side.

Imam Ahmad recorded from Ibn 'Abbas — with Abu Dawud collecting a similar narration — that these verses came down about two groups among the Jews. In the days of Jahiliyyah one group had defeated the other and imposed a treaty: fifty Wasaq of gold in blood money (diyah) for every dead person from the defeated group killed by the victors, but a hundred Wasaq for every dead person the defeated group killed from the victors. The treaty held until the Prophet ﷺ came to Madinah and both groups became subservient under him. Then the mighty group suffered a casualty at the hands of the weaker and demanded their hundred Wasaq — and the weaker group found its voice: "How can two groups who have the same religion, one ancestral lineage and a common land, have a Diyah that for some of them is half of that of the others? We only agreed to this because you oppressed us and because we feared you. Now that Muhammad has come, we will not give you what you asked." War was almost rekindled, but they agreed to seek Muhammad's ﷺ judgement. The mighty group, knowing privately that their claim was oppression — "They have said the truth anyway, for they only gave us this amount because we oppressed and overpowered them" — sent hypocrites to sound out his verdict in advance, with instructions to accept it only if it favoured them. Allah informed His Messenger ﷺ of their matter and their plot, and these ayat came down.

A separate narration, recorded by Ibn Jarir — and also by Ahmad, Abu Dawud and An-Nasa'i — names the tribes: ayah 42 was revealed concerning the blood money dispute between Banu An-Nadir and Banu Qurayzah. The dead of Banu An-Nadir were honored more and received the full diyah, while Qurayzah received only half for their dead. When they referred to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, he "compelled them to adhere to the true judgement in this matter and made the Diyah the same for both groups."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports the fuller background from al-Baghawi. Banu Nadir, the stronger and wealthier of the two tribes, had forced Banu Qurayzah — who "had no choice but to go along with it" — into a disgraceful pact: if a Nadir man killed a Qurayzah man, there was no retaliation, only seventy Wasaq of dates in blood money; but if a Qurayzah man killed a Nadir man, the killer would be executed *and* double blood money taken — one hundred and forty Wasaq of dates. The inequality ran through everything: for a Nadir woman killed, a Qurayzah man would be killed in retaliation; for a Nadir man, two Qurayzah men; if one hand of a Nadir man was cut, two hands of a Qurayzah man would be cut, and if one ear, two ears. When the Prophet ﷺ migrated to Madinah and a Qurayzah man killed a Nadir man, Banu Nadir demanded the doubled diyah, and Banu Qurayzah refused on the plea that they were of the same family, same country and same religion, and would no longer tolerate the injustice pressed on them because of their weakness. War loomed; then it was decided to take the matter to the Prophet ﷺ — but Banu Nadir first sent a group of Jews who kept up a hypocritical show of Islam to find out his view before the case was heard, with the mandate to accept his word only if it favoured their demand.

**The adultery case.** A man and woman from the Jews committed adultery. Ibn Kathir explains that the Jews had changed the law in their Book from Allah on this matter — from stoning to death to a hundred flogs and making the offenders ride a donkey facing the back of the donkey.
